pos: n. (extreme anguish of body or mind; the struggle preceding death)
etymology: Greek agonia, from agon, a contest or wrestling-place — the arena. The word is athletic before it is medical: an agony is a struggle, not merely a pain endured.
biblical_def: The word occurs once in all of Scripture, and Luke spends it on the garden: “And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground” (Luk 22:44). Everything in the sentence matters. It is an agonia — the Greek word for a contest in the arena — so this is not passive suffering but a struggle, the Second Adam wrestling where the first man yielded in a garden. And the effect of the agony is that He prayed more earnestly; anguish drove Him further into prayer rather than out of it. The petition itself is on record: “Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done” (Luk 22:42). Hebrews describes the same hour: “in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared” (Heb 5:7). What was dreaded was not the nails but the cup — the wrath due to the sin He was about to bear, for “he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities” (Isa 53:5). The agony of Gethsemane is therefore part of the atonement, not merely its prelude.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines agony as in strictness, the pain of contending in the games; hence, extreme pain of body or mind; anguish; the pangs of death; and the sufferings of Christ in the garden.
webster_full: AG'ONY, n. [Gr. a contest with bodily exertion; a word used to denote the athletic games, in Greece.]
1. In strictness, pain so extreme as to cause writhing or contortions of the body, similar to those made in the athletic contests in Greece.
2. Extreme pain of body or mind; anguish; appropriately, the pangs of death, and the sufferings of our Savior in the garden of Gethsemane.
Being in an agony, he prayed more earnestly. Luke 22.
3. Violent contest or striving.
scriptures: Luke 22:44
And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground.
Luke 22:42
Saying, Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.
Hebrews 5:7
Who in the days of his flesh, when he had offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, and was heard in that he feared;
Isaiah 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
corruption_summary: Gethsemane is read as fear of physical death, which makes Christ less brave than His own martyrs and empties the cup of its content.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard liberal reading treats the agony as a very human dread of execution, and the difficulty is immediate: Stephen went to his stoning singing, and Polycarp to the fire without a tremor. If the cup were merely death, the Master would be the least composed of His own witnesses. The Reformed answer is the only one that honours the text — the cup is the cup of wrath, the curse due to the sins He was about to have imputed to Him, and no creature has ever had to drink it. “He hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin” (2Co 5:21). That is what made the Sinless One sweat.

A second corruption comes from the devotional side and is gentler but still costly: Gethsemane preached purely as an example of submission under pressure, a model for the believer's hard night. The submission is real and is indeed a pattern — not my will, but thine, be done. But if the agony is only exemplary, the believer is left with a model and no atonement. Scripture puts the substitution first and the example second, in that order, because only a finished substitution makes the example bearable. The Christian follows a Lord who has already drunk what he himself will never taste.
roots_summary: Greek agonia (G74), a contest, agony; agon (G73), the arena, a struggle; ektenesteron (G1617), more earnestly, stretched out.
roots_lines: Greek agonia (G74) — the struggle of the contestant in the arena; Luke 22:44, and nowhere else in the New Testament.
Greek agon (G73) — the contest itself; the same root Paul uses for the good fight in 2 Timothy 4:7.
Greek ektenesteron (G1617) — more intensely, stretched out further; the agony drove Him deeper into prayer.
Greek poterion (G4221) — cup; Luke 22:42, the Old Testament figure for the portion of wrath, as in Psalm 75:8.
Greek thrombos (G2361) — a clot, a thick drop; Luke's physician's word for the falling sweat.
usage: “Being in an agony he prayed more earnestly” — anguish drove Him further in, not out.
“Remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will” — the dread and the submission in one sentence.
“Strong crying and tears… and was heard in that he feared” — heard, and not spared.

etymology: From the prefix a- and fresh, Saxon fersc. A single occurrence in the Authorized Version, in one of the most solemn warnings in the New Testament.
biblical_def: The word appears once, in the great warning passage of Hebrews: those who fall away cannot be renewed again unto repentance, “seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame” (Heb 6:6). The force of the adverb is everything. The apostate does not merely neglect the cross; by his defection he ranges himself with those who put Christ on it, and does so again, publicly, after having tasted what he now repudiates. The people described are remarkable — “once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost” (Heb 6:4) — which is why the passage has troubled readers for centuries. The Reformed reading holds that these are the privileges of the visible church, real and tasted, without the root of true regeneration; the same epistle's writer is confident of “better things” of his readers in the very next verses. The theological hinge is the impossibility of repeating the sacrifice: “Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many” (Heb 9:28), and therefore “if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins” (Heb 10:26). There is no second cross to go back to.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines afresh as anew; again; over again; after intermission.
webster_full: AFRESH', adv. [a and fresh.]
Anew; again; after intermission.
They crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh. Heb. 6.
The word denotes a repetition of that which had been done before, as if newly begun.
Fresh is from the Saxon fersc, new, not stale.
scriptures: Hebrews 6:6
If they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, and put him to an open shame.
Hebrews 6:4
For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost,
Hebrews 10:26
For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins,
Hebrews 9:28
So Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many; and unto them that look for him shall he appear the second time without sin unto salvation.
corruption_summary: The Mass claims to re-present the one sacrifice; Hebrews says the only thing offered afresh is the shame of the apostate.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome teaches that the Mass is the same sacrifice of Calvary, offered again in an unbloody manner, and Trent anathematized those who denied it. Hebrews is written against precisely this instinct. Christ was once offered (Heb 9:28); the priests of the old covenant stood daily because their work was never finished, and this Priest sat down because His was. The one thing the epistle describes as happening to Christ afresh is what the apostate does to Him — a re-crucifying in contempt, not a re-offering in devotion. That is a severe irony and it is the text's own.

On the Protestant side the passage has been abused in the opposite direction, to terrorize tender consciences into believing that a season of backsliding has forfeited salvation forever. The men described in Hebrews 6:4-6 are deliberate, public, final repudiators — they put Him to an open shame — not believers who have sinned grievously and want to come back. The mark of the reprobate here is that he does not want to return; the very desire for repentance is evidence the warning is not describing you. Perseverance of the saints and the seriousness of this warning stand together: God keeps His own, and one of the means by which He keeps them is warnings exactly this sharp.
roots_summary: Greek anastauroo (G388), to crucify again or afresh; paradeigmatizo (G3856), to make a public example; hapax (G530), once for all.
roots_lines: Greek anastaurountas (G388) — crucifying again; Hebrews 6:6, with ana- carrying the sense of repetition.
Greek paradeigmatizontas (G3856) — holding up as a public spectacle; the open shame of the same verse.
Greek hapax (G530) — once, once for all; Hebrews 9:28, the word that forecloses any repetition of the sacrifice.
Greek geusamenous (G1089) — having tasted; Hebrews 6:4, a real experience of the heavenly gift.
Saxon fersc — fresh, new; Webster's root behind the English adverb.
usage: “Crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh” — and put Him to an open shame.
“Christ was once offered” — and a finished sacrifice cannot be repeated.
“There remaineth no more sacrifice for sins” — there is no second cross to return to.

pos: pp. (transformed in appearance; changed as to outward form)
etymology: Latin transfigurare, from trans-, across, and figura, shape — a change carried across the form. It renders the Greek metamorphoo, whence English metamorphosis.
biblical_def: Matthew and Mark each use the word once, of the same six days and the same mountain. “And was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light” (Mat 17:2); “And after six days Jesus taketh with him Peter, and James, and John, and leadeth them up into an high mountain apart by themselves: and he was transfigured before them” (Mar 9:2). The crucial word is before them. Nothing was added to Christ on the mountain; the veil of His ordinary appearance was drawn back and three men were permitted to see what had been true all along. The transfiguration is therefore not a change in the Son but a disclosure to the disciples, and Peter understood it as evidentiary: “we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2Pe 1:16). Its timing is pastoral — it comes immediately after the first plain announcement of the cross, as though the Father would let three men see the glory before they watched the shame. The same Greek verb is used of the believer: “we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2Co 3:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines transfigure as to transform; to change the outward form or appearance; and particularly, the supernatural change in the personal appearance of our Savior on the mount.
webster_full: TRANSFIG'URE, v.t. [L. trans and figura, form.]
1. To transform; to change the outward form or appearance.
2. Particularly, to change the appearance of Christ on the mount, when his face did shine as the sun.
And was transfigured before them. Matt. 17.
TRANSFIGURA'TION, n. A change of form or appearance; particularly the supernatural change in the personal appearance of our Savior.
scriptures: Matthew 17:2
And was transfigured before them: and his face did shine as the sun, and his raiment was white as the light.
Mark 9:2
And after six days Jesus taketh with him Peter, and James, and John, and leadeth them up into an high mountain apart by themselves: and he was transfigured before them.
2 Peter 1:16
For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
2 Corinthians 3:18
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
corruption_summary: The transfiguration is treated as a visionary experience in the disciples' minds rather than a disclosure of what Christ objectively is.
corruption_paragraphs: Historical-critical treatments regularly classify the transfiguration as a misplaced resurrection appearance or a legendary accretion, and popular preaching often reduces it to a mountaintop experience — a template for spiritual highs and the difficulty of coming back down. 2 Peter 1:16 answers the first directly and with unusual heat: not cunningly devised fables, but eyewitnesses. Peter was on the mountain, he wrote about it decades later, and he anticipated exactly the charge that would be made. The event is offered in Scripture as testimony, not as devotional atmosphere.

The doctrinal loss in the reduction is Christological. If nothing objective happened, then the glory was generated by the observers, and the crucial truth of the passage evaporates — that the shining was His, veiled in the incarnation and briefly unveiled. Chalcedon guards this: one Person, two natures, without confusion or change. The divine glory was not acquired on the mountain and not abandoned at its foot. And 2 Corinthians 3:18 gives the believer his share, which is not a mountaintop feeling but a slow change into the same image — from glory to glory, by the Spirit, mostly in the valley.
roots_summary: Greek metamorphoo (G3339), to change form; morphe (G3444), form, essential shape; Latin transfigurare, to change across the shape.
roots_lines: Greek metemorphothe (G3339) — He was transformed; Matthew 17:2 and Mark 9:2, the root of English metamorphosis.
Greek morphe (G3444) — form as expressing essential nature, distinguished from schema (G4976), outward fashion.
Greek metamorphoumetha (G3339) — we are being transformed; 2 Corinthians 3:18, the same verb of the believer, in the passive and continuous.
Greek megaleiotes (G3168) — majesty, magnificence; 2 Peter 1:16, Peter's word for what he saw.
Latin trans- and figura — across the shape; Webster's root, and the source of the English.
usage: “Was transfigured before them” — the change was in what they were permitted to see.
“Not cunningly devised fables… but were eyewitnesses” — offered as testimony.
“Changed into the same image from glory to glory” — the believer's share, and mostly in the valley.

pos: n. (a cloth for wiping; in the Gospel, the servant's linen Christ girded Himself with)
etymology: Old French toaille, from a Germanic root meaning to wash. Twice in Scripture, both in one paragraph of John 13, and the object is a badge of office — the office of a slave.
biblical_def: John records the towel twice in two verses, and the deliberateness of the account is the point. “He riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments; and took a towel, and girded himself” (Joh 13:4). Then: “After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded” (Joh 13:5). Every clause is a deliberate act — rose, laid aside, took, girded, poured, began to wash, wiped. In that household the foot-washing was the work of the lowest slave present, and there was none, and no disciple would volunteer; so the Lord of glory put on the badge of the office. John has already told us He did it knowing that the Father had given all things into His hands, which makes the act an expression of His authority rather than a suspension of it. And He binds it on His church: “If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet” (Joh 13:14). The towel is the visible form of the great self-emptying: He “made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant” (Php 2:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines towel as a cloth used for wiping the hands and for other purposes.
webster_full: TOW'EL, n. [Fr. touaille; It. tovaglia.]
A cloth used for wiping the hands and for other purposes.
Took a towel and girded himself. John 13.
Towel of state, a long napkin formerly used at table.
The word is of Germanic origin, from a root signifying to wash.
scriptures: John 13:4
He riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments; and took a towel, and girded himself.
John 13:5
After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded.
John 13:14
If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet.
Philippians 2:7
But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:
corruption_summary: Servant language has become the standard vocabulary of Christian leadership while the towel itself is rarely picked up.
corruption_paragraphs: No word is more common in contemporary ministry than servant, and few acts are rarer than the one John describes. The corruption is not hypocrisy exactly; it is the substitution of a posture for a task. A servant-leader conference, a servant-leader title, a platform from which servanthood is taught — John 13 offers none of these. It offers a specific job that nobody in the room wanted, done by the one man with the most right to refuse. The test the passage supplies is unglamorous and local: is there a task in this congregation that the senior man will actually do because no one else will?

There is also a sacramental corruption running the other way. Some traditions have made foot-washing a third ordinance, and while the practice can be edifying, the New Testament nowhere treats it as the church ordained it treats baptism and the Supper. The Reformed position keeps the commanded ordinances two and keeps John 13:14 as a binding command about the manner of life among brethren rather than a rite. Ritualizing the towel is one more way of not using it, since a ceremony once a year is easier than a habit.
roots_summary: Greek lention (G3012), a linen cloth, towel; diazonnumi (G1241), to gird about; niptar, basin; Latin linteum, linen.
roots_lines: Greek lention (G3012) — a linen towel, borrowed from Latin linteum; John 13:4-5, and nowhere else in the New Testament.
Greek diezosen heauton (G1241) — He girded Himself; the same verb used of a slave's working dress.
Greek nipter (G3537) — the basin; also found only here in the New Testament.
Greek morphen doulou (G3444, G1401) — the form of a slave; Philippians 2:7, the doctrine the towel enacts.
Greek ekenosen (G2758) — He emptied Himself; the same verse, and the ground of the whole scene.
usage: “Took a towel, and girded himself” — the badge of the lowest slave in the house.
“Ye also ought to wash one another's feet” — a manner of life, not a rite.
“Took upon him the form of a servant” — the towel is that doctrine made visible.

pos: n. (a broad piece of linen; in Acts, the vessel let down from heaven in Peter's vision)
etymology: Saxon scyte, a sheet, from sceatan, to shoot or extend — something spread out. In Acts it translates othone, a large piece of sail-linen.
biblical_def: Both occurrences describe the same vision, told twice because Luke wanted it on record twice. “And saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners, and let down to the earth” (Act 10:11); and Peter's own retelling to the circumcision party at Jerusalem: “I was in the city of Joppa praying: and in a trance I saw a vision, A certain vessel descend, as it had been a great sheet, let down from heaven by four corners; and it came even to me” (Act 11:5). The sheet held all manner of beasts, clean and unclean together, and the command was to kill and eat. Peter refused three times, and three times was answered: “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” (Act 10:15). The vision was not finally about diet. Its interpretation arrives at Cornelius's door and Peter states it himself: “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons” (Act 10:34). The four corners are the four quarters of the earth; the ceremonial wall that separated clean from unclean has been taken down by the One who built it, and the Gentiles are in. This is the hinge on which the book of Acts turns, and it took a sheet, a trance, and three refusals to turn it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sheet as a broad piece of cloth; a broad piece of linen used in beds; a broad piece of paper; and any thing expanded, as a sheet of water or of fire.
webster_full: SHEET, n. [Sax. scyte, from sceatan, to shoot, to extend.]
1. A broad piece of cloth; a broad piece of linen used in a bed.
2. A broad piece of paper.
3. Any thing expanded; as a sheet of water; a sheet of fire.
A certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners. Acts 10.
scriptures: Acts 10:11
And saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners, and let down to the earth:
Acts 11:5
I was in the city of Joppa praying: and in a trance I saw a vision, A certain vessel descend, as it had been a great sheet, let down from heaven by four corners; and it came even to me:
Acts 10:15
And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.
Acts 10:34
Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:
corruption_summary: Acts 10:15 is now quoted to abolish God's moral law, when the vision abolished a ceremonial wall by the authority of the Lawgiver Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: “What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” has become the favourite proof text of affirming theology, deployed to argue that what an earlier age called sin should now be received. The argument fails on the text's own terms in two ways. First, the distinction removed was ceremonial — the dietary and separation laws that fenced Israel from the nations until Messiah came — and the New Testament nowhere treats the moral law of the Decalogue as similarly abrogated; Acts itself, in chapter 15, keeps the moral prohibitions in force for Gentile believers. Second, and decisively, the wall came down by direct divine revelation to an apostle, confirmed by the Spirit falling visibly on Cornelius's household, and ratified by the whole church in council. That is not a precedent any modern movement can invoke; it is the opposite of one.

The corruption in the other direction is a Judaizing instinct that never quite accepts the sheet at all — retaining dietary rules, feast obligations, or ethnic priority as though the middle wall of partition still stood. Peter's threefold refusal shows how deep that instinct runs in a genuinely godly man, and how much it took to root out. The lesson for the church is the one Peter drew: God is no respecter of persons. The sheet came down by four corners because the gospel was going to all four quarters, and no congregation may re-knit a wall Christ took apart.
roots_summary: Greek othone (G3607), fine linen, a sail-cloth; skeuos (G4632), a vessel; koinos (G2839), common, unclean; Saxon scyte, a sheet.
roots_lines: Greek othonen megalen (G3607) — a great linen sheet, the word used of ship's sailcloth; Acts 10:11 and 11:5.
Greek skeuos (G4632) — a vessel, container; the same word Paul uses of chosen instruments in Acts 9:15.
Greek koinou (G2839) — common, and so ceremonially defiled; Acts 10:15, what Peter must no longer call it.
Greek ekatharisen (G2511) — God has cleansed; the divine act that precedes the prohibition on judging.
Greek prosopoleptes (G4381) — a respecter of faces; Acts 10:34, Peter's conclusion from the sheet.
usage: “A great sheet knit at the four corners” — four corners for four quarters of the earth.
“What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common” — ceremonial, and by direct revelation.
“God is no respecter of persons” — Peter's own interpretation of his own vision.

pos: n. (as much as a penny will buy; the value of a penny)
etymology: From penny and worth. In the Authorized Version penny renders the Greek denarion, a Roman coin worth a labourer's day wage — so two hundred pennyworth is most of a year's work.
biblical_def: Both occurrences record the disciples doing arithmetic in front of the Bread of Life. Mark: “He answered and said unto them, Give ye them to eat. And they say unto him, Shall we go and buy two hundred pennyworth of bread, and give them to eat?” (Mar 6:37). John gives the same sum to Philip: “Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little” (Joh 6:7). The figure is not rhetorical. A penny was a day's wage for a labourer, so two hundred pennyworth is roughly eight months' earnings, and Philip's point is that even that sum would only yield a little apiece. He is not being faithless in the arithmetic; he is being accurate. His error is that he was asked a question by Someone for whom the calculation was irrelevant — John notes that Christ said it to prove him, for He Himself knew what He would do. Then Andrew produces the real inventory: “There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?” (Joh 6:9). The account closes with twelve baskets over. Between the pennyworth and the baskets lies the whole distance between resources and the Lord of them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pennyworth as as much as is bought for a penny; and hence any small quantity, or a good bargain.
webster_full: PEN'NYWORTH, n.
1. As much as is bought for a penny.
2. Any purchase; any thing bought or sold for money.
3. A good bargain; as, to buy a thing at a pennyworth.
4. A small quantity. Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them. John 6. The penny of the Authorized Version is the Roman denarius, a day's wages for a labourer.
scriptures: Mark 6:37
He answered and said unto them, Give ye them to eat. And they say unto him, Shall we go and buy two hundred pennyworth of bread, and give them to eat?
John 6:7
Philip answered him, Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little.
John 6:9
There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?
Matthew 6:3
But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth:
corruption_summary: The feeding is reduced to a parable about sharing, which turns a miracle of creation into a lesson in generosity and loses the point of the arithmetic.
corruption_paragraphs: The favourite liberal rendering of the feeding of the five thousand is that the crowd had food hidden in their cloaks and Christ's example moved them to share it — the real miracle being one of generosity. The pennyworth is what defeats that reading. John records the exact sum because the Evangelist wants the reader to know that the resources were counted, found insufficient by a wide margin, and that the counting was invited by Christ specifically to prove Philip. A story about shared lunches would not need the audit, and it would not need the twelve baskets of surplus at the end. The apostolic church preached a Christ who creates bread, which is why John builds the whole discourse on the bread of life out of it.

There is a practical corruption for churches too, and it is the Philip habit. Confronted with a work God has plainly commanded, the first instinct is to total the resources, compare them to the need, and conclude the thing cannot be done — and the arithmetic is usually correct. Philip was right about the money. Andrew was closer, because he at least brought the five loaves to Christ while admitting what they were worth. The dictionary's counsel is not to despise the accounting; stewardship requires it. It is to remember Whose hands the accounts are put into afterwards.
roots_summary: Greek denarion (G1220), the Roman denarius, a day's wage; diakosion denarion, two hundred pence; artos (G740), bread, a loaf.
roots_lines: Greek denarion (G1220) — the Roman denarius; Matthew 20:2 fixes it as a day's wage for a labourer in the vineyard.
Greek diakosion denarion artoi (G1250, G1220) — two hundred denarii of loaves; Mark 6:37 and John 6:7, some eight months' wages.
Greek peirazon auton (G3985) — proving him; John 6:6, the question was a test with the answer already settled.
Greek brachu ti (G1024) — a little something; Philip's estimate of each man's portion even at that price.
Greek kophinous (G2894) — the twelve wicker baskets of fragments that closed the account.
usage: “Two hundred pennyworth of bread” — eight months of a labourer's wages, and Philip was right.
“What are they among so many?” — Andrew brought them anyway.
“That every one of them may take a little” — accurate arithmetic, wrong question.

pos: interrog. adv. (Aramaic: why; the second word of the cry from the cross)
etymology: Aramaic lema / Hebrew lamah, why, to what end. The Authorized Version preserves it untranslated in both Gospel accounts, then gives the English immediately after — a rare and deliberate doubling.
biblical_def: Lama is the Aramaic word for why, and it survives in English Bibles because two Evangelists refused to translate the cry away. “And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mat 27:46); and Mark, with the Aramaic form of the divine name, “Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Mar 15:34). The Spirit preserved the actual syllables, so that the church would always have the cry in the tongue it was uttered in. And the words are a quotation: they open the twenty-second Psalm, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?” (Psa 22:1) — a psalm that goes on to describe pierced hands and feet and parted garments a thousand years before the event. The why is therefore not the cry of a man who has lost his theology; it is the Son taking a psalm of the Messiah on His lips at the exact hour it was written for. Its answer is given by Paul: “he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him” (2Co 5:21). That is why.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this Aramaic particle; lama is the interrogative why, preserved untranslated in Matthew 27:46 and Mark 15:34 and rendered into English in the same verses. (The unrelated English noun lama, a Tibetan priest, is a different word entirely and no part of the Authorized Version.)
webster_full: LAMA, in the Authorized Version, is not an English word but a transliterated Aramaic particle, lema, corresponding to the Hebrew lamah, why or wherefore.
It is preserved untranslated in the cry from the cross, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani, and then rendered by the Evangelists themselves: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me.
The words are the opening line of the twenty-second Psalm, quoted by our Lord at the ninth hour.
Readers should note that the English noun lama, denoting a priest of Tibet, is an unrelated word of Tibetan origin and occurs nowhere in Scripture.
The Evangelists' practice of giving the Aramaic and the translation together is found also at Talitha cumi and Ephphatha, in Mark 5 and 7.
scriptures: Matthew 27:46
And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Mark 15:34
And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Psalm 22:1
To the chief Musician upon Aijeleth Shahar, A Psalm of David. My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?
2 Corinthians 5:21
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.
corruption_summary: The cry is read either as despair that disproves Christ's deity or as mere recitation that empties it of pain; Scripture allows neither.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberal and unitarian readings take the cry as evidence that Jesus was an abandoned man whose confidence failed — a human tragedy with no atonement in it. Against that stands the fact that He is quoting, deliberately, the psalm that had predicted this scene in detail, and that He addresses God as My God twice while asking the question. A man in unbelieving despair does not begin with a possessive. The forsaking was real and judicial: the Son bore the penalty due to imputed sin, and was treated as the sin He was made to be. It was not a rupture in the Trinity, which cannot be divided, but the Mediator enduring the wrath owed to His people.

The opposite and more pious-sounding error is to defuse the cry by saying He was only reciting a psalm, as though the words cost nothing and the darkness were stage-setting. That empties Golgotha as surely as the first error. Both the agony in the garden and the cry from the cross tell the church what the cup contained. The Reformed have refused to soften either, because the comfort of the gospel depends on the horror being real: He was forsaken, so that those in Him never will be. The lama is the believer's guarantee that his own question will never have to be asked.
roots_summary: Aramaic lema, why; Hebrew lamah (H4100), why, wherefore; Aramaic shebaqtani, thou hast forsaken me; Hebrew azabtani (H5800).
roots_lines: Aramaic lema / Hebrew lamah (H4100) — why, to what purpose; the interrogative preserved in both Gospel accounts.
Aramaic sabachthani, from shebaq — thou hast forsaken, left, abandoned me; the Hebrew of Psalm 22:1 is azabtani (H5800).
Hebrew Eli (H410) — my God; Matthew's form, which the bystanders mistook for a call to Elijah.
Aramaic Eloi — my God; Mark's form, nearer the common speech of Galilee.
Hebrew Aijeleth Shahar (H365) — the hind of the morning; the superscription of the psalm He quoted.
usage: “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?” — preserved in the tongue it was cried in.
“My God, my God” — twice possessive, in the hour of forsaking.
“Made him to be sin for us” — the answer to the why.

pos: n. pl. (deeds of charity; acts of mercy done to the poor)
etymology: From alms, Saxon aelmesse, contracted from Greek eleemosune, mercy, pity, from eleos, mercy — and deeds. The compound insists that mercy is something done.
biblical_def: The word occurs once, and it is an epitaph: “Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did” (Act 9:36). Luke could have written that she was known for her kindness. Instead he writes good works and almsdeeds which she did — and then the narrative shows the widows standing around her body holding up the coats and garments she had made. That is what almsdeeds look like in the record: cloth, cut and sewn, for women with no husband to provide. The compound word itself is the doctrine, since mercy in Scripture is never an attitude that stops short of a deed. The angel says as much to Cornelius: “Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God” (Act 10:4) — prayers and alms rising together, neither one standing alone. And the Lord fixes the manner: “when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth” (Mat 6:3). Dorcas is the pattern exactly: her almsdeeds were unknown enough that they had to be displayed by weeping widows after she died.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines almsdeed as an act of charity; a charitable gift; and alms as what is given gratuitously for the relief of the poor.
webster_full: ALMS'DEED, n. amz'deed. An act of charity; a charitable gift.
ALMS, n. amz. [Sax. aelmesse; Gr. eleemosune, from eleos, mercy.]
Any thing given gratuitously to relieve the poor, as money, food, or clothing, otherwise called charity.
A pious man is to be known by his alms-deeds.
This woman was full of good works and alms-deeds which she did. Acts 9.
scriptures: Acts 9:36
Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did.
Acts 10:4
And when he looked on him, he was afraid, and said, What is it, Lord? And he said unto him, Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God.
Matthew 6:3
But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth:
James 1:27
Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.
corruption_summary: Mercy has been professionalized and publicized — delegated to institutions and reported for credit — which removes both the deed and the secrecy.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 6:3 forbids the left hand knowing what the right hand does, and the modern charitable economy is built on the opposite principle: the giving is announced, branded, and counted, because visibility raises more. The corruption is not that organized relief is wrong — the Jerusalem collection was organized, audited, and carried by approved men. It is that the individual Christian's own hands have largely been retired from the work. Dorcas made the coats herself. A cheque discharges a bill; it does not by itself produce the thing Luke thought worth an epitaph.

There is also a doctrinal caution. Acts 10:4 says Cornelius's prayers and alms came up as a memorial before God, and Rome has read such texts as evidence that alms merit favour — the treasury of merit rests on this instinct. But Cornelius was not saved by his alms; the angel's next instruction is to send for Peter, who must tell him words whereby he shall be saved. God noticed his mercy and answered it by sending him the gospel. Almsdeeds are the fruit of faith and the evidence of pure religion (Jas 1:27); they have never been its purchase price.
roots_summary: Greek eleemosune (G1654), alms, mercy shown; eleos (G1656), mercy; agathon ergon (G18, G2041), good works; Saxon aelmesse.
roots_lines: Greek eleemosunon hon epoiei (G1654) — almsdeeds which she did; Acts 9:36, with the relative clause insisting on the doing.
Greek eleos (G1656) — mercy; the root of eleemosune, and of the English alms by long contraction.
Greek mnemosunon (G3422) — a memorial; Acts 10:4, the sacrificial word for the portion that ascends.
Greek Dorkas (G1393) — a gazelle; the Greek rendering of the Aramaic Tabitha.
Saxon aelmesse — alms; Webster's root, worn down from the Greek across a thousand years.
usage: “Full of good works and almsdeeds which she did” — and the widows held up the coats.
“Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial” — the two ascend together.
“Let not thy left hand know” — which is why Dorcas needed weeping widows to publish hers.

pos: n. (a preacher of the gospel; one of the offices Christ gave to His church)
etymology: Greek euangelistes, from euangelion, good news, from eu-, well, and angello, to announce. An evangelist is simply a man whose work is the announcing of good news.
biblical_def: The New Testament uses the noun three times and never defines it abstractly; it points at a man and at a task. Luke names the man: “we entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, which was one of the seven; and abode with him” (Act 21:8) — the same Philip who had been chosen to wait on tables in Acts 6, then “went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them” (Act 8:5), and was sent to a single Ethiopian on a desert road. Paul names the office among Christ's ascension gifts: “he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers” (Eph 4:11). And he lays the work on a settled pastor who was not himself an itinerant: “watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry” (2Ti 4:5). Note the company that command keeps — watchfulness and the enduring of afflictions on either side of it. Evangelism in the apostolic vocabulary is a labour under hardship, not a temperament and not an event, and every minister of the word is charged with its work whether or not he holds the title.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines evangelist as a writer of the history of Jesus Christ; and a preacher or publisher of the gospel of Jesus Christ, not fixed in any place but travelling as a missionary.
webster_full: EVAN'GELIST, n.
1. A writer of the history or doctrines, precepts, actions, life and death of Jesus Christ; as the four evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John.
2. A preacher or publisher of the gospel of Jesus Christ, authorized by divine commission.
In the primitive church, evangelists were preachers not fixed in any place, but travelling to preach the gospel.
Do the work of an evangelist. 2 Tim. 4. From euangelion, good news.
scriptures: Ephesians 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
2 Timothy 4:5
But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry.
Acts 21:8
And the next day we that were of Paul's company departed, and came unto Caesarea: and we entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, which was one of the seven; and abode with him.
Acts 8:5
Then Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them.
corruption_summary: The evangelist has been reinvented as a platform personality measured by crowds and decisions, an office the New Testament would not recognize.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern celebrity evangelist — itinerant, independent of any congregation's oversight, sustained by the size of his meetings and the count of his decisions — is a nineteenth-century American invention, and the machinery that came with it has done real damage: the manipulated appeal, the altar call engineered like a sales close, the counting of professions as conversions. Philip is the apostolic picture, and the scale is instructive. He preached to a city in Samaria and to one man in a chariot, and Scripture gives the single convert as much space as the city. An evangelist under the New Testament is answerable to a church, and his success is not a number.

The opposite corruption is peculiarly Reformed and should be named plainly. Because we rightly hold that God effectually calls His elect, some have grown content to let evangelism happen and to treat any organized zeal for it as suspicious. 2 Timothy 4:5 is a command to a settled pastor: do the work of an evangelist. Sovereign grace ordains means as surely as ends, and preaching is the chief of them. A doctrine of election that cools a man toward the lost has been misunderstood; it was the doctrine that drove Whitefield and Judson and Spurgeon, and it produced more missionaries than it ever excused.
roots_summary: Greek euangelistes (G2099), a bringer of good news; euangelion (G2098), gospel; euangelizo (G2097), to announce good news.
roots_lines: Greek euangelistes (G2099) — an announcer of good news; found only at Ephesians 4:11, Acts 21:8, and 2 Timothy 4:5.
Greek euangelion (G2098) — good news, gospel; from eu-, well, and angelia, a message.
Greek euangelizo (G2097) — to proclaim glad tidings; the verb Philip is doing throughout Acts 8.
Greek ergon poieson euangelistou (G2041) — do the work of an evangelist; a labour, not a title.
Greek plerophoreson (G4135) — fill full, make full proof of; the same verse, of the whole ministry.
usage: “Some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers” — a gift of the ascended Christ.
“Do the work of an evangelist” — said to a settled pastor, between watching and enduring afflictions.
“Philip the evangelist, which was one of the seven” — a city, and one man in a chariot.

pos: n. (the time of evening; the hour toward the close of day)
etymology: From evening and tide, Saxon tid, meaning time or season rather than the sea — as in Whitsuntide, eventide, noontide. The word means simply evening-time.
biblical_def: Scripture uses eveningtide twice, and both are hours when something is decided. The first is a king at leisure: “And it came to pass in an eveningtide, that David arose from off his bed, and walked upon the roof of the king's house: and from the roof he saw a woman washing herself” (2Sa 11:2). It is the hour that begins the worst chapter of David's life, and the narrative is careful to note he was on a roof at evening when he should have been at the war. Idleness at eveningtide is where the fall started. The second is Isaiah's oracle against the plunderers of Judah: “And behold at eveningtide trouble; and before the morning he is not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us” (Isa 17:14). Trouble at evening, and by dawn the enemy has ceased to exist — God's judgment executed inside a single night. So the two uses set the hour's two possibilities: a man's guard drops at evening, and God's deliverance also comes at evening. The disciples on the Emmaus road knew the hour as the time to ask for company: “Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent” (Luk 24:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eventide as the time of evening; evening; and notes that tide in such compounds signifies time or season.
webster_full: E'VENTIDE, n. [even and tide, time.] The time of evening; evening.
In an eveningtide David arose from off his bed. 2 Sam. 11.
TIDE, n. [Sax. tid, time, season.] Time; season. In this sense it is obsolete, except in composition; as in Whitsuntide, noontide, eventide.
And behold at eveningtide trouble. Is. 17.
The compound denotes simply the season or hour of evening, not the flowing of the sea.
scriptures: Isaiah 17:14
And behold at eveningtide trouble; and before the morning he is not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us.
2 Samuel 11:2

And it came to pass in an eveningtide, that David arose from off his bed, and walked upon the roof of the king's house: and from the roof he saw a woman washing herself; and the woman was very beautiful to look upon.
Luke 24:29
But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them.
1 Peter 5:8
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What has been lost is the ordering of the day itself — the evening hour that once belonged to family worship now belongs to the screen.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is a plain compound and nobody is contesting it. What has quietly changed is the practice attached to the hour. In the Puritan household eveningtide was a fixed appointment — the father gathered the house, read a portion, sang, and prayed — and 2 Samuel 11:2 is the standing argument for why the hour needs a governor. David had nothing to do at evening and no one to answer to, and he was the most powerful man in Israel. A man's guard is lowest when the work is done, the house is quiet, and nothing is required of him.

The principle to recover is the ordered evening. Isaiah 17:14 shows the same hour as the time of God's deliverance, and Luke 24:29 as the hour the risen Christ was constrained to stay and was known in the breaking of bread. Evening is not a spiritually neutral stretch of time to be filled with whatever is nearest. It is the hour Scripture associates both with the deepest danger and with the nearest fellowship, which is exactly why 1 Peter 5:8 pairs sobriety with vigilance and puts a lion in the field. Family worship at eveningtide is not nostalgia; it is a posted watch.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'eth ha'ereb (H6256, H6153), the time of evening; lipnoth 'ereb, at the turning toward evening; Saxon tid, time or season.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'ereb (H6153) — evening, the going down of the light; the same word that begins each day in Genesis 1, the evening and the morning.
Hebrew le'eth 'ereb (H6256) — at evening time; Isaiah 17:14, and the hour of the evening sacrifice.
Hebrew le'eth ha'ereb — 2 Samuel 11:2, the hour David rose from his bed and walked on the roof.
Greek pros hesperan (G2073) — toward evening; Luke 24:29, the Emmaus request.
Saxon tid — time, season; Webster's root, surviving in Whitsuntide and noontide.
usage: “In an eveningtide, that David arose from off his bed” — the hour the fall began.
“At eveningtide trouble; and before the morning he is not” — judgment inside one night.
“Abide with us: for it is toward evening” — and He went in to tarry with them.
